lesson.title: Graphing the Integral Itself
lesson.summary: An accumulation function F(x) is not just a running total, it is an ordinary function with its own graph, and because F'(x) equals f(x), the sign and shape of the integrand f directly control where F increases, decreases, and turns around.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter treated F(x) = the integral from a to x of f(t) dt as a running total, a quantity accumulating over time. Step back from that physical framing for a moment and treat F simply as a function like any other, with its own graph, its own increasing and decreasing stretches, and its own local maxima and minima. The question becomes: what does that graph look like, and can you figure it out just by studying f, without ever writing down an explicit formula for F?

You can, and the tool is exactly FTC part one. Since F'(x) = f(x), everything the first derivative test tells you about a function applies directly, with f playing the role of F's derivative. Wherever f(x) is positive, F is increasing, because F is adding positive area as x moves forward. Wherever f(x) is negative, F is decreasing, because F is adding negative, signed area. Wherever f(x) crosses from positive to negative or back, F has a critical point, a local maximum or minimum, the same way any function has a critical point where its derivative changes sign. None of this requires knowing an explicit closed form for F. Reading the graph of f is enough to sketch the essential shape of F.

Here is a worked example. Let f(t) = t - 2, and define F(x) = the integral from 0 to x of (t - 2) dt. An antiderivative of t - 2 is t^2/2 - 2t, so F(x) = x^2/2 - 2x. Differentiating confirms F'(x) = x - 2, matching f(x) exactly. Now analyze F using f's sign: f(t) = t - 2 is negative for t less than 2 and positive for t greater than 2, so F is decreasing on (0, 2) and increasing afterward, meaning F has a local minimum at x = 2. Evaluate it directly: F(2) = 4/2 - 4 = 2 - 4 = -2. Check this geometrically: on [0, 2], the graph of f runs from (0, -2) up to (2, 0), entirely below the axis, forming a triangle with base 2 and height 2, so its signed area is -(1/2 times 2 times 2) = -2, matching F(2) exactly.

The analysis can go one derivative further. Since F'(x) = f(x), it follows that F''(x) = f'(x), so the concavity of F is controlled by whether f itself is increasing or decreasing. For this example, f(t) = t - 2 is increasing everywhere, so F''(x) = 1 is always positive, meaning F is concave up everywhere, consistent with x^2/2 - 2x being an upward opening parabola. Treating the integral as a genuine function, worthy of the full graphing toolbox rather than just a running total, is what this chapter adds to the accumulation function idea introduced just before it.
